rv.q: It is remarkable how the playwright is able to pack so many aspects of her cultural heritage so easily within a surprisingly traditional father-and-daughter story.

rv.q: And yes, King of the Yees does dip toward the sentimental at the end. But it's so clever, so metatheatrical, and so affectionate throughout that I hardly minded.
King of the Yees is less of a traditional family play and more of a formal experiment, one that's at times confounding but never boring, and sure to leave you with more questions than answers.
Act 2 moves like a freight train, but director Joshua Kahan Brody doesn't let things get out of control.

cn.t: Lauren Yee's meta-theatrical comedy about Chinese American identity in San Francisco's Chinatown earns mixed-to-positive reviews for its inventive family portrait, though its hazy, layered storytelling proves more successful for some than others.
